usage: the verb 갈아입다 'change clothes' is the natural partner, not just 입다
underwear is counted with 벌, the counter for clothing sets
면(綿) names the fabric; 면 + garment is a fixed modifier pattern

examples: 속옷을 매일 갈아입어요.

갈아입다 (change-into) is the habitual verb; plain 입다 sounds like a first-time action
속옷이 다 젖었어요.

새 속옷을 사야 하는데 어디 가지요?

nuance: 속옷 is the umbrella word for anything worn directly against the body under your outer clothes — it transparently breaks down as 속 'inside, inner part' + 옷 'clothes', so literally 'inner clothes'. It covers both men's and women's items and is the neutral term you'd use shopping or at home; in clinical or marketing contexts you may also meet the Sino-Korean 내의(內衣, 'inner-garment') for thermal underwear specifically. The crucial trap for English speakers is the verb: although you 'wear' underwear in English, the everyday Korean verb is 갈아입다 ('change into') because underwear is something you swap daily, and the counter is 벌 (one 속옷 한 벌), never 개. Do not confuse 속옷 with 잠옷 (pajamas) or 수영복 (swimsuit) — those are worn over the body for a purpose, while 속옷 stays hidden underneath.

usage: 으로 marks the result you change into; 갈아입다 is the natural verb at bedtime
바람으로 = 'wearing only ~', stressing you're underdressed to go out

-은 채로 = 'in the unchanged state of', i.e. without taking it off
examples: 밤에는 잠옷을 입어요.
At night I wear pajamas.

잠옷이 너무 편해서 벗기 싫어요.

-아서 gives the reason; 벗다 'take off' is the opposite of 입다
잠옷 차림으로 편의점에 다녀왔어요.

nuance: 잠옷 literally stacks 잠 'sleep' (the noun from 자다 'to sleep') + 옷 'clothes', so 'sleep-clothes' — clothes whose whole job is to be comfortable in bed. It overlaps with the borrowed 파자마 (pajamas) and the broader 실내복 ('indoor wear', 室內服), but 잠옷 specifically frames the garment around sleeping, while 실내복 is any loungewear you'd relax in awake. Register is fully neutral and casual. The English-speaker pitfall is cultural rather than grammatical: in Korea wearing 잠옷 outside the home reads as notably sloppy, so the phrases 잠옷 바람으로 / 잠옷 차림으로 ('in just your pj's') carry a faintly embarrassed nuance. Grammatically remember the opposite of 입다 ('put on') is 벗다 ('take off'), and use the clothing counter 벌, not 개.

usage: I dress up in a suit.
차려입다 ('dress up smartly') is the verb that matches formal wear
a jacket-and-trousers set is counted as 한 벌, since 벌 means a full matching set

검은색 정장에 흰 셔츠가 제일 무난해요.

nuance: 정장 is Sino-Korean 正裝, literally 正 'proper, correct' + 裝 'attire' — 'correct/proper dress', i.e. the formal outfit appropriate for serious occasions (interviews, weddings, funerals, important meetings). It overlaps with 양복(洋服, 'Western clothes'), but there is a real dividing line: 양복 names the Western-style tailored garment as a thing (and skews masculine and slightly old-fashioned), whereas 정장 names the formal register of the outfit and applies equally to men's and women's formal wear. The opposite is 캐주얼 or 평상복 ('everyday clothes'). The English-speaker pitfall is counting and the verb: a suit is one matched set, so 정장 한 벌 (not 한 개), and the natural verb is 입다 or, for the 'dress up' feel, 차려입다 — never 신다, which is only for footwear.

borrowed style adjectives like 스키니 sit directly in front of 청바지

nuance: 청바지 = 청(靑) 'blue/indigo' + 바지 'trousers', literally 'blue trousers' — the 청 element is what specifically marks denim, since plain 바지 just means 'pants' of any kind. It's the standard, completely neutral word for jeans across all ages and is far more common in speech than the English loan 진/데님 (데님 normally refers to the fabric, not the finished garment). Casual register, never formal. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: first, jeans are grammatically singular in Korean — 청바지 한 벌 / 한 개, never a plural form — so you don't 'wear a pair'; second, the verb is 입다 ('put on the lower body'), and a tight or loose fit is described with 끼다 ('snug/tight') or 헐렁하다 ('loose'), not the English 'tight'. Pair it naturally with 티셔츠 or 운동화 for the default casual look.

usage: tops take 입다; 를 marks the object

티셔츠가 줄어들어서 동생 줬어요.

이 티셔츠 목이 늘어났어요.

nuance: 티셔츠 is a direct loanword from English 'T-shirt' (named for its T shape), and it specifically means a pull-over knit top — most often short-sleeved cotton. The key contrast English speakers miss is 티셔츠 vs 셔츠: in Korean 셔츠 by itself implies a button-up collared shirt (a dress shirt / 와이셔츠), so a casual tee must keep the 티 to stay distinct. Sleeve length is built right into the noun phrase: 반팔 티셔츠 (half-sleeve) vs 긴팔 티셔츠 (long-sleeve). Register is casual and neutral. The pitfalls: (1) the verb is 입다, never 신다; (2) thin tees are frequently counted with 장 ('흰 티 한 장' = one plain white tee), though 벌 also works for an outfit; and (3) Koreans clip it to 티 in speech (흰 티, 검은 티), so don't be thrown when the 셔츠 disappears.

usage: knit tops take 입다; 를 marks the object
목폴라 'turtleneck' specifies the collar type before the noun
보풀이 일어나다 'form lint balls/pills' is the set phrase for knitwear pilling

examples: 날씨가 추워서 스웨터를 꺼냈어요.
It got cold, so I took out a sweater.
-아서 reason; 꺼내다 'take out' (of storage) fits seasonal clothes
스웨터 안에 셔츠를 받쳐 입어요.
I layer a shirt under the sweater.
받쳐 입다 'wear underneath as a layer' is the exact verb for layering
이 스웨터는 따뜻한데 좀 따가워요.
This sweater is warm but a bit itchy/prickly.
-는데 contrasts the two qualities; 따갑다 'prickly' is what wool feels like on skin
nuance: 스웨터 is a loanword from English 'sweater' and names a warm knitted pullover top for cold weather. It sits in a tight cluster of near-synonyms you should separate: 니트 (from 'knit') is the broad fashion word for any knitted top and is currently more trendy in clothing shops; 가디건 (cardigan) is the open-front, button-up knit you wear like a jacket; 스웨터 leans toward the closed pull-over you slip over your head. So a buttoned knit is 가디건, not 스웨터. Register is neutral/casual. Pitfalls for English speakers: (1) the verb is 입다, and layering under it is 받쳐 입다; (2) describe wool's feel with 따갑다 ('prickly') or warmth with 따뜻하다, not a borrowed word; (3) count with 벌, and remember knit care vocabulary like 보풀 (pilling) and 손빨래 (hand-wash) that comes up constantly when shopping for one.

usage: a one-piece garment takes 입다; 를 marks the object
무늬 'pattern' attaches to a noun: 꽃무늬 'flower pattern'

season + garment is a fixed modifier pattern
examples: 오늘은 원피스를 입었어요.
Today I wore a dress.

이 원피스 너무 예쁜데 좀 비싸요.
This dress is so pretty, but it's a bit pricey.
-는데 sets up the 'but'; 예쁘다 is the ㅡ-irregular adjective for 'pretty'
결혼식에 입을 원피스를 하나 사려고요.
I'm going to buy a dress to wear to the wedding.

nuance: 원피스 is a loanword from English 'one-piece', and that literal sense is the whole point: it's a dress where top and skirt are a single connected garment, as opposed to a 투피스 ('two-piece', a matching top-and-skirt set). The sharp contrast English speakers must learn is 원피스 vs 드레스: everyday casual or work dresses are 원피스, while 드레스 in Korean is reserved for a formal gown — a wedding dress (웨딩드레스) or evening gown — so calling your sundress a 드레스 sounds like you're going to a gala. The word is essentially female-coded. Register is neutral. Pitfalls: (1) the verb is 입다; (2) compliment the fit with 어울리다 ('it suits you'), the single most useful clothes-shopping verb; (3) count with 벌, and (4) never split a 원피스 into separates — that's literally a 투피스.

살이 빠져서 벨트를 한 칸 더 조였어요.
I lost weight, so I tightened my belt one more notch.
살이 빠지다 'lose weight'; 조이다 'tighten'; 칸 = a notch/slot
이 벨트는 정장에도 잘 어울려요.
This belt goes well even with a suit.
에도 'even with'; 어울리다 for matching accessories to an outfit
nuance: 벨트 is a loanword from English 'belt' — the strap worn around the waist to hold up trousers or as an accent, very often leather (가죽). A more traditional native synonym exists, 허리띠 (허리 'waist' + 띠 'band/sash'), which sounds plainer and a touch old-fashioned; in fashion and shopping contexts 벨트 dominates. The single most important point for English speakers is the verb. You do NOT 입다 a belt; you 매다 ('tie/fasten') or, very commonly, 하다 (벨트를 하다 'put a belt on'), and you take it off with 풀다 ('undo'). This 매다/하다 pattern is the same one used for 넥타이 and 스카프 — accessories you fasten rather than slip your body into. Tightening or loosening is counted in 칸 (notches): 벨트를 한 칸 조이다/풀다. Count belts with 개 (벨트 한 개), since they're individual objects, not garment sets.

usage: 매다 'tie/knot' (or 하다) is the verb for a tie — never 입다
I loosen / take off the tie.
풀다 'undo' is the natural opposite of 매다
무늬 'pattern' → 줄무늬 'stripe pattern' modifies the noun
고쳐 매다 'fix and re-tie' = adjust a crooked knot
examples: 출근할 때 넥타이를 매요.
I put on a tie when I go to work.
-(으)ㄹ 때 'when'; 매다 is the correct verb for tying it
넥타이가 좀 비뚤어졌어요.
The tie has gone a little crooked.
비뚤어지다 'become crooked/askew' is the verb for a knot slipping out of line
면접 때문에 넥타이를 새로 하나 샀어요.
Because of the interview, I bought a new tie.
때문에 'because of'; 하나 'one (item)'; ties are bought for formal occasions
nuance: 넥타이 is a loanword from English 'necktie' — the long strip of cloth knotted at the neck of a dress shirt, standard in business and formal wear and largely male-associated. Korean has no everyday native equivalent, so 넥타이 (often clipped to 타이 in fashion contexts) is simply the word. The decisive thing for English speakers is again the verb: a tie is fastened, so you 매다 ('tie/knot') it or use the catch-all 하다 (넥타이를 하다), and you undo it with 풀다 — using 입다 here is a classic beginner error, because 입다 is strictly for garments you put your torso or legs into. This is the same 매다/하다/풀다 family as 벨트 and 스카프. Adjusting a crooked knot is 고쳐 매다 or describing it as 비뚤어지다 ('go askew'). Count ties with 개 (넥타이 한 개), not the clothing-set counter 벌.

usage: 하다 is the everyday verb for wearing accessories — not 입다
걸다 'hang' fits literally, since a necklace hangs from the neck
진주 'pearl' names the material before the noun
어울리다 'suit/match' for jewelry paired with an outfit
examples: 오늘은 목걸이를 했어요.
Today I put on a necklace.
은 on 오늘 marks the contrast with usual; 하다 → 했어요 is the natural past
생일에 친구한테서 목걸이를 받았어요.
I got a necklace from a friend for my birthday.
한테서 'from (a person)'; 받다 'receive' — necklaces are a common gift
목걸이 줄이 끊어졌어요.
The necklace chain snapped.
줄 'chain/string'; 끊어지다 'snap/break (of a line)' is the exact verb for a chain breaking
nuance: 목걸이 is, unusually for this list, a pure native Korean word, transparently built from 목 'neck' + 걸이, a noun from 걸다 'to hang' — so literally 'a neck-hanger', the thing you hang around your neck. That etymology is also a memory hook for the verb: you can 걸다 ('hang') a necklace, though the most common everyday verb for putting on any accessory is simply 하다 (목걸이를 하다). The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 입다 ('wear'), which only works for clothing you put your body into; jewelry takes 하다/걸다, removed with 풀다 or 빼다. Register is neutral. Watch the family of related neck/ear words that share 걸이 or a body part: 귀걸이 (ear-ring, 귀 'ear' + 걸이) and 팔찌 (bracelet) all take 하다, not 입다. Count with 개 (목걸이 한 개), and note that the cord is the 줄, which can 끊어지다 ('snap').

usage: 끼다 'insert (onto a finger)' is the dedicated verb for rings — not 입다 or even 하다
빼다 'pull out/remove' is the natural opposite of 끼다
커플 + item names matching rings worn by a couple
The ring fits the finger perfectly.
딱 맞다 'fit exactly' for ring sizing
examples: 약지에 반지를 껴요.
I wear a ring on my ring finger.
약지 'ring finger'; 에 marks where; 끼다 is the verb
반지가 너무 꽉 껴서 안 빠져요.

꽉 끼다 'fit too tightly'; -아서 reason; 빠지다 'come off/slip out'

-(으)ㄹ 때 'when'; 주다 'give'; rings carry the engagement meaning here too
nuance: 반지 is the everyday word for a finger ring, a piece of jewelry worn for decoration or as an engagement/couple symbol (커플 반지, 결혼 반지). The verb is the headline for English speakers, and it's special: rings take 끼다 ('to insert/slip onto'), because you slide your finger through them — not 입다 (clothing), not even the general accessory verb 하다 that 목걸이 and 벨트 use. So 반지를 껴요 ('I put on a ring'), removed with 빼다 ('pull out'); a too-tight ring 꽉 끼다 and won't 빠지다 ('come off'). This 끼다 also governs other finger/face items you thread or slot on — 장갑을 끼다 (gloves), 안경을 끼다 (glasses) — so learning it here pays off broadly. Register is neutral. Count rings with 개 (반지 한 개), and place them with 에 on a finger: 손가락에/약지에 반지를 끼다.
